How your payoff works

Here's how your payoff works. When you pay off your Homeshare, you pay back a set share of your home's value at that time, and that share is shown at the top of this panel. So your payoff moves with your home: if its value rises, your payoff rises, and if its value falls, your payoff falls too. There's also a ceiling. Your payoff can never grow faster than the annual cost limit, so in the early years, that limit is usually what sets your payoff. After that, your share of the home's value takes over, and your annual cost tends to come down the longer you keep it. Use the slider to choose the year you might pay it off, and the buttons to try different home values. Every year is listed in the table just below.

The full explanation

A Homeshare gives you cash now in exchange for a percentage of your home's value when you sell, refinance or pay it off. There are no monthly payments, and it isn't reported to the credit bureaus. You have up to 10 years, and you can pay it off at any time with no prepayment penalty. An annual cost limit caps what you could ever owe, so your payoff can never grow faster than that limit allows.

A Homeshare is a good fit if you want cash without monthly payments and are comfortable paying it back later. It isn't the right fit if you need a fixed monthly payment, want the lowest possible rate, or aren't comfortable paying it back within the term.

You can pay off your Homeshare at any time with no penalty, and it works just like a mortgage payoff handled by the title company. If you sell your home, it's settled at closing from the sale. At the end of the 10-year term, you have three options: sell the home, refinance, or start a new Homeshare with another 10-year term.
